events.text: A child in a river village has not slept for a month. Every night something comes out of the window of that house, a shape of smoke with too many teeth, and every night the child screams, and the whole lane lies awake. You are lying in the reeds across the river. The shape smells of nothing you have ever eaten. You are hungry anyway.

choices.text: Lie down under the window and draw it in

effects.log: You lie down under the window, a hill that has learned to be quiet, and when the shape comes out you draw it in through your trunk like smoke from a pipe. It goes down cold and bitter and then it is gone. Inside, the child sighs, turns over, and sleeps until noon. The old books will say you eat bad dreams. Tonight, for the first time, you did. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Put your trunk to the shutter and listen first

effects.log: You listen. The shape is made of a flood: the child saw a house go down the river last summer, with someone still on the roof. You understand it the way you understand iron, from the inside. Then you eat it, slowly, the whole flood. The child sleeps. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Stay in the reeds: it is not iron

effects.log: You stay in the reeds. It is not iron, and you do not know what it would do to you. The child screams until dawn. You lie there listening to all of it, and in the morning you are not sure you were right.

events.text: The taste stays with you for a year. Iron tastes of the hands that held it: a farmer's sweat on a hoe, a soldier's fear on a spear. A nightmare tastes of nothing, and then, a long time after, of the person who is not having it any more. You find you want that taste more than any sword.

choices.text: Go looking for the next one

effects.log: You go down the river at night, house by house, listening at the shutters. A fisherman's drowning. A widow's empty bed. A boy's war that has not happened yet. You eat them all, and the river towns sleep, and nobody knows why. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Think about why it fills the tail, and not the belly

effects.log: Iron fills the Belly. This fills the tail, where the rice is, where the last of your maker's hands are. You lie a whole season thinking about that. Your maker, you decide, would have eaten bad dreams too, if anyone had shown how.

events.text: The child who could not sleep is grown, and has walked three days up the river to find you. A bowl of rice is set down on a flat stone in front of your trunk, and a spoon of good brass beside it. "For the thing that eats bad dreams," the grown child says, to the air, not quite to you. "My grandmother always said."

choices.text: Eat the rice. Leave the spoon

effects.log: You eat the rice, grain by grain. You do not touch the spoon. The grown child sees that and laughs out loud, and goes home, and from then on in that village they leave a bowl for you, and never a spoon. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Eat the spoon, as a joke

effects.log: You eat the spoon. The grown child stares, then laughs so hard there are tears. "Grandmother said you would do that," comes the voice, through the laughing. You eat the rice too. (Rice +1)

events.text: The river village asks you to stay. The headman says it in front of everyone, very formally, with the elders behind: a winter, a year, as long as you like. The village has had no smith since the old one died, and its forge stands cold. The headman knows what you are. The headman asks anyway.

choices.text: Stay one winter, and eat their bad dreams

effects.log: You stay one winter, curled around the village like a wall. Nobody in it has a bad dream from the first snow to the thaw. In spring, when you go, the children run after you to the edge of the paddies, and stop there, as told. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Teach them to leave a bowl, and go

effects.log: You go. But first you lie outside the headman's door for one night and eat the headman's worst dream, so the headman will remember you properly. In every village down the river, now, there is a bowl at the foot of a chimney on cold nights.

choices.text: Leave an anvil from your Belly on the headman's step

effects.log: You open your jaws, and an anvil comes out, cold and black, a little smaller than it was. The headman looks at it for a long time. Then the whole village laughs, and the smith's grandchild picks up a hammer. (Rice +3)

events.text: A fever has come to the river towns. The doors have straw ropes across them, the old ward against sickness, and the markets are shut, and every evening a cart goes down to the burning-ground with straw over what it carries. You can taste the fever in the air from a ridge away. It tastes of rust gone wrong.

choices.text: Lie across the main road and eat the bad air all night

effects.log: You lie across the main road from dusk to dawn and draw in the sick air through your trunk, street by street. It sits in you like a stone. You are ill for a month, which has not happened to you in all your long life. But in the town, the carts stop. (Rice +3, -8 health)

choices.text: Ask the town shaman where the fever came in

effects.log: The shaman will not come out of the house, but talks to you through the straw rope. "It came up the river on a boat," comes the answer. "Eat it at the landing." You eat it at the landing, all one night, and the fever turns back like a boat that has lost its oars. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Keep away: they are frightened enough

effects.log: You keep to the ridge. They are frightened enough without a hill-sized beast in the road. Over the river you hear the carts every evening. It is a long summer.

events.text: {npc}, a shaman from the town, has climbed the ridge with a brush and a pot of cinnabar and a yellow paper charm, and is standing in front of your face in the morning mist, very small, reaching up. The charm is for you. It is the charm that is pasted on doors to keep out what you are.

choices.text: Lower your head and let the charm be pasted on

effects.log: You lower your head, the whole hill of it, and {npc} pastes the charm on your forehead, between your small eyes. Then {npc} sits down on your trunk and does not leave until dark, talking about the fever, the town, the river. Nobody has sat with you like that in a long time. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Blow the charm gently away

effects.log: You blow, very gently. The charm flutters off down the ridge. {npc} watches it go and laughs, the first laugh in that town for a month. "Well," comes the verdict, "it was worth trying." They talk till noon.

events.text: The fever comes back in the autumn, stronger, as fevers do when they have been beaten once. It is in three towns at once now, up and down the river, and you are one beast, however large.

choices.text: Walk the river all night, every night, eating it

ok.log: You walk the river bank all night, every night, for forty nights, from one town to the next, eating the fever out of the air before it can settle. On the forty-first night there is nothing left to eat. (Rice +3)

fail.log: You walk the river all night, every night, and cannot be in three towns at once. Two of them you save. The third buries a great many people that autumn, and you lie on the hill above it and listen to the bells. (-6 health)

choices.text: Ask the three towns to come to you

effects.log: You send word by the shaman: come to the hill. They come, in carts and on stretchers, the whole sick river, and lie down in your shadow, and for a month you breathe in nothing but fever. It is the worst month of your long life. It works. (Rice +3, -10 health)

events.text: The straw ropes come down from the doors. In the river towns, that spring, somebody paints you on a door: a bear with an elephant's trunk and a hide of needles, very badly, eating a little black cloud. By summer every door in the valley has one.

choices.text: Go and look at the paintings

effects.log: You walk down the main road in daylight, very slowly, looking at yourself on every door. The trunk is always too short. The eyes are always kind. Nobody runs. A child stands beside one of the paintings and points from it to you and back. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Stay on the ridge, and let the doors keep the town

effects.log: You stay away. The doors are enough; that is what doors are for. In a hundred years, nobody in the valley will know why the beast is painted there. Every family will still paint it.

events.text: A court lady comes out of the capital with a lantern and two terrified guards and stands at the foot of your hill. The court that once hunted you with torches is asking you in. The queen has not slept in a year, the lady says. The physicians have tried everything. The old books say you eat bad dreams.

choices.text: Go with the lantern

effects.log: You follow the lantern into the capital at midnight, down streets that were never made for anything your size. The guards walk very fast. Every shutter on the way opens a crack.

choices.text: Ask why the court should trust you now

effects.log: "Because we have nothing else," the lady says, honestly, and that is the best answer anyone at court has ever given you. You go.

choices.text: Refuse: they hunted you

effects.log: You refuse. The lady bows and goes back with the lantern. You lie awake all night thinking about a queen who cannot sleep, which is not what you meant to do.

events.text: The queen's hall is too small for you, so you lie in the courtyard and put your trunk to the latticed door. Inside, a single lantern, court ladies kneeling, and the queen lying very still with her eyes open. What comes out of the lattice at the second watch is not smoke. It is fire: a palace burning, again and again, the same night.

choices.text: Eat the fire in the dream

effects.log: Fire is food to you now, even dreamed fire. You draw it out through the lattice, the whole burning palace of it, hall by hall. When it is gone, the queen closes her eyes. The court ladies do not dare move until dawn. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Eat it slowly, and learn what she fears

effects.log: You eat it slowly, and learn it: a palace that burned in a war long ago, and a fear that it will burn again with her in it. You leave a little of the fear behind, the useful part, the part that keeps a queen awake to fires. (Rice +2)

events.text: The ministers of war have heard that the Iron-Eater is in the palace. They want you chained there: a guard no army can pass, they say, an armoury that walks. The armourers have heard it too, and have locked every spear in the city in the cellars, and are sitting on the doors.

choices.text: Let the ministers try to chain you

effects.log: They bring chains. You eat them. They bring bigger chains. You eat those. By the third day the ministers have run out of chains and the armourers have stopped sitting on the cellar doors and are laughing at the ministers. You go home.

choices.text: Tell them you came for one queen's sleep, not their wars

effects.log: You say it in the voice of an old general whose sword is in you somewhere, and the ministers go white, because they knew that general. Nobody mentions chains again.

events.text: The queen sleeps, now, and has sent for you once more, by day. She asks, through the lattice, what you want. The court has gold, land, a title for a beast if you like. The ladies are holding their breath to hear the answer.

choices.text: Ask for a bowl of rice

effects.log: A bowl of rice, you say. The queen laughs, the first time anyone at court has heard it in a year, and has it brought, and watches you eat it from behind the lattice. In the palace kitchens, ever after, one bowl is cooked each day for nobody. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Ask for the palace's broken iron

effects.log: You ask for the palace's broken iron: bent hinges, cracked pots, nails from roofs that fell. It is brought in forty carts, and the court thinks you a very cheap beast. (Rice +1)

choices.text: Ask for nothing, and go

effects.log: Nothing, you say, and go. The queen sits a long time behind the lattice. The court chroniclers write that the beast asked for nothing, and underline it, because nobody at court has done that in living memory.

events.text: The great palace of the capital has lain in ruins for generations, since the war in which every palace burned. Now the regent is rebuilding it, all of it, at once: timber from every mountain, stone from every quarry, and nails. Ten thousand carts of nails. The builders have heard of you. They are very nervous about the nails.

choices.text: Keep away from the building site

effects.log: You keep to the hills north of the city and watch the palace go up, roof by roof, over the years. Not one nail goes missing. The builders leave a cart of bent ones at the foot of your hill each autumn, as thanks.

choices.text: Give them iron from your Belly for their nails

effects.log: You walk to the smiths' yard at the edge of the site and open your jaws, and out comes iron: old swords, old ploughs, a temple bell. The smiths stare, and then they set to work, and the palace is nailed together with what you ate. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Lie on the ridge and watch, chewing a stone

effects.log: You watch. You chew a stone, which is not iron, out of habit. The builders watch you watching. In the end everyone gets used to it, and the work goes on.

events.text: At the palace's great gate the masons set up two stone beasts on plinths, facing south toward the fire mountain across the river: Haechi, the fire-wards, the ones who judge. They are carved in granite, with a horn and a bell, and they are only stone. When you pass the gate at dusk, one of them seems to be looking at you.

choices.text: Lie down beside the stone ones for a night

effects.log: You lie down beside the gate between the two plinths. The stone does not move. In the morning there is frost on both of them and none on the ground between, where you lay. The gatekeepers decide this is a good sign.

choices.text: Bow to them, as one fire-eater to another

effects.log: You bow your great head to the stone ones. Nothing happens. Then something does: a breath of cold, as if from far away, as if somewhere a real one with a real horn had looked up from its own business and nodded. You do not see it. You do not need to.

choices.text: Ask the stone what it judges

effects.log: You ask. Stone does not answer. But you think about it all night: what you have eaten, and whose it was, and what a creature with a horn for the guilty would make of you. In the morning you look at your own belly differently. (Rice +2)

events.text: Behind the queen's quarters the builders have made a terraced garden on a little artificial hill, and on it, four chimneys of orange brick, six-sided, with longevity symbols set in the brick: cranes, deer, pines, the sun. The underfloor fires of the hall draw through them. At night sparks come up out of them, and you are hungry for sparks.

choices.text: Lie in the garden and eat the sparks

effects.log: You lie down along the terraces and eat the sparks as they come up, every night of the winter, so not one of them lands on a palace roof. The queen's ladies say there is a warm hill in the garden that was not there before. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Eat what comes down the flue, too

effects.log: Bad things come down chimneys, the old people say: evil qi, bad dreams, what the cold brings. You lie at the foot of the chimneys and eat what comes down as well as what goes up. The queen's quarters have the quietest winter in the palace. (Rice +3)

events.text: {npc}, a mason with a chisel and a bag of soft stone, has come into the garden at dawn and is looking at you the way masons look at a good block. "The chimneys have cranes and deer and pines," comes the explanation, "and nothing at the bottom. I want you at the bottom. Will you sit?"

choices.text: Sit very still for a whole season

effects.log: You sit. You are good at sitting. {npc} works all spring, with the chisel going tap, tap, tap, and every evening stands back and frowns and goes on. In summer the little carving is finished: a bear with a trunk and a hide of needles, at the foot of the chimney, eating a cloud. It is you. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Fidget, and be carved fidgeting

effects.log: You fidget. You cannot help it; it is spring, and there are sparks. {npc} laughs and carves you fidgeting: one ear up, the trunk curled, as if about to sneeze. It is the liveliest thing on the whole chimney.

choices.text: Decline: you are not a decoration

effects.log: You decline. {npc} shrugs, and carves a crane at the bottom instead, a perfectly good crane. You find you mind more than you expected.

events.text: {npc} is old now, and comes into the garden with a stick instead of a chisel, and sits down by the carving at the foot of the chimney. "It will outlast me," comes the remark, "and the palace, maybe. A little stone you, eating the sparks going up and the bad dreams coming down. You could stay with it, you know. Some things are worth staying for."

choices.text: Go back to the hills, and come when the palace needs you

effects.log: You stay with {npc} until the sun goes down, and then you go back to the hills. You will come when the palace needs you. The little stone one can keep the chimney until then.

choices.text: Come back every winter for the sparks

effects.log: Every winter, from then on, you come back to the garden and lie at the foot of the chimney, beside yourself. {npc} lives to see four of those winters. The ladies of the palace come to expect you, like snow. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Stay, and become the carving

effects.log: You lie down at the foot of the chimney, very small, smaller than you have been in an age, and when {npc} looks again there is only the carving: a bear with a trunk, eating a cloud. It is a little warmer than the brick around it, always. The sparks go up and do not land. The bad dreams come down and do not arrive.

events.text: The queen dowager's hall in the palace has burned and been rebuilt, and its chimney is not a chimney at all but a piece of the garden wall pushed out, with the ten longevity symbols set into it in brick: the sun, mountains, water, clouds, rocks, pines, turtles, deer, cranes, the herb of long life. Above them, bats and cranes. Below them, at the very bottom, a pair of little iron-eaters.

choices.text: Look at the pair at the bottom a long time

effects.log: Two of you, side by side, the size of a cat each, carved in brick at the foot of the wall. Nobody told the makers that there is only one of you. You find you like being two. (Rice +1)

choices.text: Ask the bricklayers why you are at the bottom

effects.log: "The cranes are for heaven," says a bricklayer, "and the bats are for luck. And you are at the bottom because bad things come in low, with the cold, through the flue. You stop them." Then, realising who has asked: "Sir. Madam. Beast."

events.text: The queen dowager is very old and has heard that the real one comes to the chimney sometimes. One winter evening she has a cushion put out on the veranda and waits, wrapped in furs, to see. You come up the garden in the dusk.

choices.text: Lie down by the wall-chimney where she can see you

effects.log: You lie down along the wall, beside your two brick selves. The old queen dowager looks at you, and at them, and says it is a poor likeness, and laughs, and asks you to stay until the lamps are lit. You stay. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Eat the cold that is coming down the flue

effects.log: A hard frost is coming down out of the north, and with it whatever comes with frost. You eat it at the foot of the wall all night. The old queen dowager sleeps on the veranda in her furs and wakes warm. (Rice +2)

events.text: Long after the old queen dowager is gone, people come to look at the chimney: scholars with notebooks, children on outings, a woman who counts the symbols and finds more than ten. They point at the cranes. Hardly anyone notices the pair at the bottom.

choices.text: Lie in the hills and be pleased nobody notices

effects.log: Nobody notices. That is how a ward should be. You lie in the hills, and the chimney stands, and nothing bad comes in low with the cold.

choices.text: Walk past at dusk, once, so somebody notices

effects.log: You walk past the wall at dusk, once. A child on an outing sees you, and then sees the pair at the bottom of the chimney, and looks back and forth, and says nothing to the teacher, and remembers it all life long.

events.text: Some nights, high above the mountains, there is a terrace of cloud among the stars. Four banners at its four sides, blue and white and red and black, and in the middle a coil of gold cloud that lies very still, as if asleep, and is not. The great ones of the four directions meet there. Nobody has ever asked you up.

choices.text: Lie on your back and watch it till dawn

effects.log: You lie on your back on the mountain, a hill looking up at the sky, and watch. Voices, very faint. Something writes. The gold in the middle does not move all night, and once, you could swear, says one word, very slowly. You never hear what.

choices.text: Call up to it, once

effects.log: You call up, once, in the voice of every sword in you. The terrace does not answer. A little later a grey clerk comes down the mountain path with a brush behind one ear, looks at you, writes something, and goes back up. You will never know what it wrote. You suspect: eats iron.

events.text: You understand, after long watching of the terrace, why you are not on its roll. The four keep the four directions, and the gold keeps the middle. You keep nothing. You were a scrap of rice once. You are what you ate.

choices.text: Decide that is enough

effects.log: It is enough. Nobody on the terrace ever ate a child's bad dream on a river bank. You turn over and sleep, and the terrace can do its own work.

choices.text: Decide to be worth a seat one day, anyway

effects.log: You decide to be worth asking, one day, even if nobody asks. It is a good thing to decide. It makes the next century go differently.

events.text: The Martial Alliance has called every sect under heaven to one hall: the orthodox and the unorthodox, the old families, the temple orders, even envoys from the Demonic Cult. There is one matter on the table. It is you. You could eat every sword in the murim, now, and the murim knows it.

choices.text: Go to the hall

effects.log: You go. It takes a week to walk there, because you walk slowly so that the roads will hold. Every village on the way has its iron locked in the cellar. Nobody needs to.

choices.text: Send word that you will come when asked properly

effects.log: You send word, by a terrified courier, that you will come when you are asked properly, not summoned. Three days later the Alliance sends an invitation on silk, with every sect's seal. You go.

events.text: You put your head in at the open doors. Inside, a hundred masters in their sect colours, and a hundred swords drawn: the blades of Mount Hua's school, the taiji swords of Wudang, the Alliance Leader's own. Every one of them is pointed at you. Every one of them, you could eat.

choices.text: Ask

effects.log: You ask. Just that: in the voice of an old master the hall remembers, you ask whether any of them would give you a sword, freely. Nobody moves. Then somebody at the back laughs, and somebody else says, "Ask what?" and the conclave, which was going to be a war, becomes an argument. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Wait in silence until they lower them

effects.log: You wait. Swords are heavy, held out for an hour. One by one the tips come down. When the last one is down you ask, quietly, whether any of them would give one. (Rice +1)

choices.text: Take the nearest one

effects.log: You take the nearest one. A blade of Mount Hua's school goes out of a master's hand and into your jaws before the master has finished the first cut. The hall erupts. You walk out with every sword in the murim pointed at your back, and you know now that they will have to be taken, one by one. (Rice -2)

events.text: The argument goes on for nine days. Some say give it the swords and it will stop. Some say it will never stop. Some say the murim is only swords, and without them they would all be farmers, which several farmers' sons in the hall think would be no bad thing. On the ninth day they turn to you and ask you to speak for yourself.

choices.text: Speak for yourself, in your own voice

ok.log: You speak in your own voice, which nobody has heard: not a sword's old owner, just you, a scrap of rice and all your years of iron. You say that you do not want their swords. You want to be given them, which is different. The hall is silent a long time. Then the old abbot of Shaolin stands up. (Rice +2)

fail.log: You speak in your own voice, and it comes out like a landslide. Half the hall draws again. You stop, and say it again more quietly, and this time they hear some of it. Enough, perhaps.

choices.text: Speak in the voice of the swords they lost

effects.log: You speak in the voices of the swords' old owners: their grandfathers, their founders, their dead. Every master in the hall hears someone they loved. Many of them weep. It is not quite fair, and it works. (Rice +1)

events.text: On the last night of the conclave you lie outside the hall, and a human comes out to you alone. It is not a master you know. It stands in front of your trunk in the dark and says one word, very quietly: a silly word, the kind a tired person gives a thing made out of their own supper. Every voice in you falls silent at once.

choices.text: Put your trunk to the ground before the human

effects.log: You put your trunk to the ground. You do not know how this human knows the word. You think, perhaps, that it does not know either: that it came from somewhere further back than this life. It goes back into the hall without another word. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Ask where the word came from

effects.log: "I do not know," the human says. "I dreamed of an attic once." Then it goes. The word stays in you, warm, at the bottom of everything. (Rice +3)

events.text: Some of the masters do not come back into the hall after the speeches. You can see one of them on the hill above the hall, sitting alone, watching. Not with a sword drawn. Just watching, all night, as if waiting to see what the others will do, and what you will.

choices.text: Look up at the hill a long time

effects.log: You look up at the hill a long time. The watcher does not move. You have the odd feeling you have been seen like this before, from a hill, by someone who would not give and would not fight. It steadies you.

choices.text: Walk up the hill and lie down beside the watcher

effects.log: You walk up the hill and lie down beside the watcher, the way a dog lies down by a fire. Neither of you says anything. In the morning the watcher goes down and gives the Alliance a sword for you, and does not stay to see it given. (Rice +2)

events.text: At dawn the Alliance Leader comes out of the hall with a sword held flat across both palms: the Alliance's own, the sword every Leader has carried. "The conclave has decided nothing," the Leader says. "So I will. This one is given, not taken. The rest, you must ask for one by one."

choices.text: Take it gently, as given

effects.log: You take it as gently as a child takes a bowl. It goes into you like coming home. The hall, watching from the doors, lets out one breath. One given. Eight to go, and every one of them must be asked for. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Ask the Leader to keep it until the others have given

effects.log: You ask the Leader to keep it until the last, so that nobody gives because the Leader did. The Leader looks at you a long time, and sheathes it, and nods. "Then come back for it," the Leader says. "At the end."

choices.text: Bow, and go out to the mountains to ask

effects.log: You bow, the whole hill of you, and go out to the mountains. The sects will be asked, one at a time, at their own gates.

events.text: You lie down across the valley below the great sects' mountains and wait. You have asked. Now you wait to see who comes down the path with a sword held out hilt-first, and who does not come at all. It may take a century. You have centuries.

choices.text: Wait, and eat nothing that is not given

effects.log: You eat nothing that is not given. It is harder than anything you have ever done: you are the size of a mountain and the hunger is the size of you. But the rice in your tail is warm, and grows warmer. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Wait, and give back what you can while you wait

effects.log: While you wait you give back: a temple bell to a temple, a magistrate's seal to a county, ploughs to a famine valley. The sects on the mountains watch you do it, year after year. (Rice +3)

events.text: An old master of Mount Hua comes down the path in the spring, in white, with plum blossom caught in the sleeves, and stops in front of your trunk. The sword is held out hilt-first: the plum-blossom blade, twenty-four cuts in one flowering. "The founder would have wanted to see what it does inside you," the master says.

choices.text: Take it, as given

effects.log: You take it. It flowers in you, all twenty-four cuts, and settles. The old master watches your hide where the hilt comes out among the needles, and nods, and goes back up the path without a word. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Ask the master to keep it one more generation

effects.log: You ask the master to keep it one more generation, for a student who is not yet good enough. The master laughs, and goes up the path, and comes back thirty years later with the student, who holds it out. You take it then.

events.text: A Daoist of Wudang comes down the mountain very slowly, practising as she walks, the taiji sword moving in her hands like water going round a stone. She does not stop practising when she reaches you. The last movement of the form ends with the sword held out to you, hilt-first.

choices.text: Take it, as the last movement of the form

effects.log: You take it as the form ends, so that the form ends in you. The Daoist bows, and turns, and begins the form again, going back up the mountain, with empty hands. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Learn the form first, then take it

effects.log: You watch the form a hundred times, until you could do it yourself, if you had hands. Then you take the sword, and it moves in you the way it moved in hers. (Rice +2)

events.text: The abbot of Shaolin comes down on foot, very old, carrying the temple's iron staff on one shoulder. "It is not a sword," the abbot says, "so it will not count for whatever you are counting. Take it anyway. It has stopped enough people. Let it rest."

choices.text: Take the staff

effects.log: You take the staff. It does not count. It is the heaviest gift you have ever been given, and the lightest to carry. The abbot sits down on your trunk to rest before the climb back, and falls asleep. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Ask the abbot to keep it for the temple

effects.log: You ask the abbot to keep it: a temple needs something to lean on. The abbot looks relieved, and then ashamed of looking relieved, and then laughs at both. "Then the temple gives you a sword instead," the abbot says, and a novice brings one down that evening. (Rice +2)

events.text: A swordsman from a small sect nobody has heard of comes down the path with a plain sword in a cloth. Nameless, the sword and the sect. "We are not famous," the swordsman says. "But it is the only sword we have, and our founder made it, and you should have it, because everyone else is giving theirs."

choices.text: Take it: it counts as much as any

effects.log: You take it, and it counts as much as any famous blade, because it was given freely and it was all they had. The swordsman walks back up the path lighter, swinging empty arms. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Give the sect something back for it

effects.log: You take it, and give back from your Belly an old general's spear, a temple bell, and a hundred ploughs for their valley. The small sect becomes, overnight, the richest in the province, and never draws a sword again. (Rice +3)

events.text: Two sects have been at war for three generations, over a river, over a grave, nobody quite remembers. Both leaders come down to you on the same morning, from opposite ends of the valley, each with a sword. "If you have both," says one, "neither of us can finish it." "Then it is finished," says the other.

choices.text: Take both swords

effects.log: You take both swords, one from each side, at the same moment. The two leaders stand in the valley with empty hands, looking at each other. Then, because there is nothing else to do with their hands, they shake them. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Take one, and make them share the other

effects.log: You take one, and leave the other lying between them. Neither leader picks it up. In the end it rusts there, in the valley, and both sects tell the story as a victory. (Rice +2)

events.text: You have taken one, and the murim will not give you the others now. Very well. There are other ways to come by a sword. The Wudang gate is one night's walk away, and a gate is only iron.

choices.text: Go and take the Wudang sword

effects.log: You go up the mountain in the night and eat the gate and then the sword out of the hall of the founder, while the Daoists stand in their courtyard in their night robes, not running, because there is no point. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Take a nameless master's sword on the road

effects.log: You take a sword off a nameless master on the road, the way a bandit would. It is easy. It does not count for anything, except against you. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Stop. Go back and ask instead

effects.log: You stop at the foot of the mountain. You go back to the valley and lie down and wait to be given, the hard way. It will take longer now. It will be worth more. (Rice +2)

events.text: The sects lock their swords in vaults of stone now, which you cannot eat but can lift. They bury them. They throw them into deep lakes. You find them anyway: a buried sword sings to you through ten feet of earth.

choices.text: Dig them up, one by one

effects.log: You dig them up, one by one, the whole spring: the buried, the drowned, the walled-up. Every one of them was somebody's. (Rice -3)

choices.text: Take the Shaolin staff from the temple

effects.log: You take the iron staff out of the temple at Shaolin while the monks chant at you. They do not stop chanting. It is the worst sound you have ever eaten through. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Leave the buried ones buried

effects.log: You leave them. Something about a sword buried by its own sect so that you would not have it makes you tired. You go and sleep in the old mine for years. (Rice +1)

events.text: The murim is changing. In the sect courtyards, disciples practise with wooden poles. The famous masters fight with their fists, and some of them are better at it than they ever were with a sword, and some of them are nothing at all. Nobody fears a sword any more. Everybody fears you.

choices.text: Take more

effects.log: You take more. Kitchen knives in the sect halls. The guards' spears at the city gates. The smiths do not bother forging new ones; you would only come. (Rice -3)

choices.text: Watch a courtyard of wooden poles a whole day

effects.log: You watch. The disciples are clumsy with the poles, and laugh at each other, and nobody bleeds. It is not what you expected. You do not know if it is better. You lie on the hill thinking about it, and take nothing that year.

choices.text: Give back half, at the sect gates, by night

effects.log: You go round the sect gates by night and leave half of what you took on their steps. In the morning the masters find their swords, and do not understand, and are more afraid of you than before. (Rice +3)

events.text: There is one famous sword left in the murim that you do not have: the one the Alliance Leader wears, on the last night, in an empty hall, waiting for you alone, without guards, because guards would only be eaten. The Leader does not draw it. "Take it, then," the Leader says, "and there is no murim any more."

choices.text: Give every sword back, at once, and go

effects.log: You open your jaws, there in the empty hall, and every sword you ever took comes out at once, ringing on the stone floor like a temple at the new year. The Leader stands up to the knees in swords, and does not move, and then begins to laugh. You go. It will be centuries before anyone gives you anything. You do not mind. (Rice +6)

choices.text: Leave the last sword where it is

effects.log: You leave it. One sword in the world. The Leader sits in the empty hall with it across both knees, and the murim, what is left of it, gathers round that one sword like a village round a well. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Take the last sword

effects.log: You take it. The Leader does not resist. The next morning, all across the land, there is not a famous sword left in any hand. Masters fight with fists and sticks, and nobody fears a sword, and everybody, from the sea to the northern rivers, fears you.

events.text: A pilgrim on the mountain road, who does not know what you are, tells you a story to pass the time: up past the third pass there is a grave nobody tends, a small mound with a stone and moss and nothing else. Somebody who made something, the village says, a long time ago, out of their own supper.

choices.text: Go up past the third pass

effects.log: You go up past the third pass, slowly, the whole mountain of you, and the pilgrim watches you go and understands, a little late, who they were talking to.

choices.text: Ask the pilgrim to tell it again

effects.log: The pilgrim tells it again, and you listen to every word. Then you go up past the third pass.

events.text: You dug your maker's grave yourself, under the pines behind the hut, a very long time ago, when you were still small enough to dig it with your claws, and could not stop crying in the way a beast cries, which is all at once and all over. You have not been back since. You find, this spring, that your feet are taking you there.

choices.text: Let your feet take you

effects.log: You let them. It is a long way and a short one. The pines behind the hut are very old now, and the hut is gone.

choices.text: Go the long way, by the river towns

effects.log: You go the long way, by the river towns, eating bad dreams as you pass, so that you arrive with something to show. (Rice +2)

events.text: The grave is very small. It would fit under one of your feet. There is a stone with no name on it, and moss, and nothing else. You lie down and put your trunk on the stone, and every voice in you, every sword's old owner, every general and master, goes quiet at once.

choices.text: Lie there a whole year

effects.log: You lie there a whole year, with your trunk on the stone, in the quiet. Snow falls on you and melts. Something at the very bottom of you, under all the iron, is listening. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Clear the moss off the stone with your trunk

effects.log: You clear the moss off the stone, very carefully, and leave a little pile of nails on the mound, because you do not know what else people leave. (Rice +2)

events.text: On the anniversary of the day you were made, which you did not know you knew, you are lying at the grave in the evening, and a word comes up out of you. Not out of the swords. Out of the rice. The word your maker said over a scrap of rice, the first thing you ever heard.

choices.text: Say it aloud at last

effects.log: You say it aloud. It is a silly word, a pet name, the kind a tired person gives a thing made of their own supper. The mountain hears it. The pines creak. All the iron in you rings, once, like a bell, and is still. (Rice +4)

choices.text: Keep it, unspoken, at the bottom of you

effects.log: You do not say it. You keep it, at the bottom of everything, under all the iron, where it has been the whole time. It is enough to know it is there. (Rice +3)

events.text: You come back to the grave, as you have every spring for years. You are very large now and very old, and the mountain is very quiet, and you could lie down here and not get up. Nobody would blame you. Nobody would even know.

choices.text: Get up, and go back to the world

effects.log: You get up. There are bad dreams in the river towns and swords that have not been given yet. You brush the leaves off the stone, and go. Your maker made you to eat, after all, and then to stop. Not yet.

choices.text: Come every spring, and leave every spring

effects.log: You come every spring and leave every spring, from then on. The village below starts leaving nails on the mound for you, for luck. You eat them on the way down. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Lie down on the grave, and never eat again

effects.log: You lie down on the grave, with your trunk on the stone, and do not get up again. You do not eat again. The rust comes, slowly, over a century, and then the moss, and then the pines, and in the end there is a long rusted mound beside a small one. Children from the village leave nails on it, for luck.

events.text: {npc} is a farmer who has brought you nails every market day for twenty years, walking up from the valley with a little sack, never asking anything. Today {npc} sits down on your foot to rest and asks one thing: "Is it true there is a way to stop you? My grandmother said. I would never. I just want to know if it is true."

choices.text: Show {him} the tail

effects.log: You curl your tail round where {npc} can see it: the pale tip, grainy, like cooked rice, the only part of you that is not iron. You say: fire, there. {npc} looks at it a long time, and then at you. "I will never," comes the answer. "Unless you ask."

choices.text: Say: yes, and not yet

effects.log: Yes, you say. And not yet. {npc} nods, as if that were a perfectly ordinary answer, and gives you the nails, and goes home. You find you trust {him} more than any master in the murim.

choices.text: Say nothing, and eat the nails

effects.log: You eat the nails. {npc} waits, and then laughs, and says it was a foolish thing to ask. It was not. You both know it.

events.text: {npc} is older, and still comes on market days, slower now. "I have been thinking," {npc} says, "about what would come out of you. If it ever happened. All of it? The ploughs, the bells, the swords?" You have been thinking about it too.

choices.text: Tell {him} everything you ever ate, one by one

effects.log: You tell {npc} everything: the first needle, the keepers' spoons, the last plough of a village, the army's halberds, the famous swords. It takes all day. {npc} listens to all of it and at the end says only, "It would all go home." Yes. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Say: I do not know. That is what frightens me

effects.log: You do not know. Perhaps it would all go home. Perhaps you would. {npc} puts a hand on your trunk and leaves it there, and does not say anything comforting, which is a comfort.

events.text: {npc} comes up the hill one evening with a torch, unlit, and sits down beside your tail and does not light it. "I am getting old," comes the explanation. "If you ever ask, it had better be soon, or it will be somebody else. I thought you should know."

choices.text: Say: not yet. Come back next year

effects.log: Not yet, you say. {npc} nods, and sits with you until it is dark, and goes home with the torch still unlit.

choices.text: Ask {him} to choose who will hold it after

effects.log: You ask {npc} to choose who will hold it after. {npc} thinks about it for a month, and brings a grandchild up the hill, very solemn, aged nine, who looks at your tail and says it looks like rice. It does. (Rice +2)

events.text: It is dusk in the field below the hill, and {npc} is there with the torch, lit this time, because you asked. The whole valley has come out to watch from the edge of the paddies. {npc} is not crying. {npc} is waiting for you to say it.

choices.text: Send {him} home. Not this year

effects.log: You put your trunk over the torch, gently, and eat the flame. Not this year. {npc} lets out a breath, and laughs, and the valley goes home disappointed and relieved. You will ask again, or you will not.

choices.text: Let {him} keep the torch, for whenever

effects.log: You tell {npc} to keep the torch, and give it to whoever comes after. There is a torch now, in a farmhouse in the valley, wrapped in oilcloth, that has never been lit. Somebody will always know. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Turn your tail to the torch

effects.log: You turn your tail to the torch. {npc} puts it to the rice, and the rice catches, and does not hurt. And out of you, all at once, it comes: the first needle, the keepers' spoons, a village's last plough, an army's halberds, the famous swords of the murim, a temple bell, ten thousand nails. It pours across the field in a river and goes home, every piece of it, to every house it was taken from. Where you were there is nothing but a few grains of rice, smoking a little, in the grass.

events.text: {npc}, a young monk from a small temple in the hills, comes to you with an old staff wrapped in cloth. "My order goes back to a monk who hid in an attic," comes the explanation, "in the last days of the old kingdom. This was the staff. Our abbots say one blow of it would make you give back everything. I did not believe them. I wanted to see you before I decided."

choices.text: Let {him} unwrap it

effects.log: {npc} unwraps it. Plain wood, worn smooth by hands, the end split. The moment you see it, every piece of iron in you turns toward it, the way needles turn north. You were made by the hands that held this. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Ask {him} to put it away

effects.log: You ask {npc} to put it away. {npc} does, quickly. But you know it is there now, in a temple in the hills, and you will never quite forget.

events.text: Your maker's staff has been kept all these centuries where you left it, and it has waited. Now there is {npc}, a young monk of your maker's line, who has come to ask about it. "The old ones say there is a staff," {npc} says, "and a blow, and a promise. Nobody alive has seen it. I would like to, before I believe it."

choices.text: Bring the staff out and give it into {his} hands

effects.log: You bring it out, and lay it across {npc}'s hands. Plain wood, worn smooth by hands, the iron tip with no toothmarks on it. {npc} holds it as if it were a sleeping child. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Tell {him} where it is, and let {him} fetch it

effects.log: You tell {npc} where it is. {npc} goes and fetches it alone, and comes back a different person, and sits down by you without a word.

events.text: {npc} comes back every year, with the staff and without it, to sit with you and talk about the old monk: what is remembered in the temple, the bowl a day, the attic, the reward on the gate. Some of it is wrong. Some of it is things you had forgotten.

choices.text: Correct the stories

effects.log: You correct them, gently: it was one bowl, not two; the keepers were kind; there was a cat. {npc} writes it all down for the temple. It is the only true account there will ever be. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Let the wrong stories stand

effects.log: You let them stand. They are better stories than what happened, and the temple loves them. {npc} looks at you sideways, once, and knows, and does not change a word.

events.text: {npc} is the abbot now, grey, and stands in the temple yard with the staff in both hands, because you asked {him} to come. "Once," {npc} says. "One blow. If you ask. I have practised it every morning for thirty years, in case."

choices.text: Say: not yet. Keep practising

effects.log: Not yet. {npc} lowers the staff, and laughs, and goes back to practising the next morning, and the morning after, as long as {he} lives. The temple will have someone practising it for a thousand years.

choices.text: Ask {him} to give the staff to the next abbot

effects.log: You ask {npc} to pass the staff on, with the blow, and never to use it unless you ask. The order of the attic monk will keep it, generation after generation, like a promise that has not been needed yet. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Bow your head, and ask for the blow

effects.log: You bow your head to the stones of the yard and ask. {npc} lifts the staff and brings it down, once, not hard, the way a teacher taps a student who has finally understood. And everything you ever ate comes out of your jaws onto the stones: needles, ploughs, bells, swords, a whole kingdom's iron, ringing. When it stops, there is nothing in the yard but a great heap of metal and a monk with a staff, and the morning.

events.text: There is a famine valley in the south where there has not been enough iron for ploughs since before anyone remembers. They scratch the fields with wooden sticks and get a third of a harvest. The smiths of the valley have nothing to forge. Somebody in that valley has written to you, in a child's hand, asking for one plough.

choices.text: Go, and give them a hundred ploughs from your Belly

effects.log: You go down to the valley and open your jaws in the smiths' yard, and out comes iron, a great deal of it. The smiths stand round it like people round a fire on a cold night. That spring there are a hundred ploughs. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Send one plough, as asked

effects.log: You send one plough, as asked, carried down by a carter who is frightened all the way. The child who wrote ploughs the family's field with it, alone, at nine years old. The valley comes to watch. (Rice +1)

events.text: The valley is a little better, and then a little worse again: ploughs wear out, the harvest is small, the children are thin. The smiths come up to your hill together, eleven of them, with their hammers, and stand there not saying what they came to say.

choices.text: Say it for them

effects.log: You say it for them: you are made of iron, a hill of it, more than this valley could use in a thousand years. They could melt you. The smiths look at the ground. "We would never ask," says the eldest. You know. (Rice +1)

choices.text: Give them more, and send them home

effects.log: You give them more, a cart each, and send them home. It will last them a good while. It is not the answer, and you all know it, and nobody says so.

events.text: The famine valley has had three bad years. The smiths' forges are cold. You lie on the hill above the valley and look down at the cold forges, and at your own vast iron flank, and the arithmetic is very simple.

choices.text: Go back to the hills

effects.log: You go back to the hills. You are not ready, and the valley would not want you to be ready because of them. You send down what you can spare, every year after. (Rice +1)

choices.text: Lie in the valley a year first, and watch the farmers

effects.log: You lie in the valley a year and watch the farmers scratch the earth with sticks. It is the longest year of your long life. At the end of it you know what you are going to do, whenever you do it. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Walk down into the forges, and let them melt you

effects.log: You walk down into the valley and lie down among the smithies, and tell the smiths to light every forge. They weep, and light them. It takes all winter. You do not mind the heat; heat was always food. That spring there are ten thousand ploughs and sickles in the valley, laid out on the ground in rows like rice seedlings, and every field is turned, and every furrow is you.

events.text: Some winters you dream of the north: past the last county, past the river, past the last of the maps, where there are no swords because there are no people, and the iron lies in the mountains untouched and unowned.

choices.text: Walk a little way north, to see

effects.log: You walk north for a month, to see. The villages thin out, then stop. The snow is very clean. You come back in spring, and are not sure why.

choices.text: Lie still and dream it

effects.log: You lie still and dream it. In the dream you are small again, the size of a calf, and nobody has heard of you.

events.text: A hunter from the far north, wrapped in furs, has come south for salt and stops at the foot of your hill. In the north, the hunter says, there are mountains of black stone with iron in them that nobody has ever dug, and nobody wants. No sects. No kings. A great deal of snow.

choices.text: Ask about the mountains

effects.log: You ask about the mountains for three days. The hunter, flattered, draws them in the snow with a stick: here a river, here a black ridge, here nothing for a month's walk. You learn the map by heart.

choices.text: Give the hunter a good knife for the road

effects.log: You give the hunter a good knife from your Belly, an old one, a general's. The hunter turns it over and over and goes north with it. (Rice +1)

events.text: Snow is falling on the north road. You are standing at the edge of the last county, where the road goes on into white and stops being a road. Behind you, the murim, the swords, the river towns, the bowls at the chimneys. Ahead, nothing at all.

choices.text: Turn back. Not yet

effects.log: You turn back. There are bad dreams in the river towns still. The north will be there.

choices.text: Go a season, and come back

effects.log: You go a season into the white, and eat nothing, and come back thin and quiet and very calm. People on the north road say you came out of the snow like a hill walking. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Walk on, past the last of the maps

effects.log: You walk on. The snow covers your footprints a little after you make them, and then the footprints are all there is, going north, and then not even those. Some say you still live, somewhere past the maps, eating the black mountains slowly and bothering nobody. Some say you will come back.

events.text: Your tail is dark grey now, like a grain left too long in the pot. When you look at it, you cannot remember why it matters. There is iron in the next valley. There is always iron in the next valley.

choices.text: Go to the next valley

effects.log: You go to the next valley and eat its iron: ploughs, pots, a temple's bell, the hinges off the doors. It is very easy. You do not remember, afterwards, whose any of it was. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Look at the tail until you remember

effects.log: You look at your tail until you remember. It takes all night. A pair of hands, a lamp, a bowl a day. In the morning you go and give back a plough. (Rice +3)

events.text: Nobody brings you nails any more. The villages have learned: they hide their iron and run when you come. There is a red sky over the fields where you have been, and the soil there is rust.

choices.text: Eat what they hid

effects.log: You find it, all of it, under the floors and down the wells. It is easy. Everything is easy now. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Lie down outside a house and eat a nightmare instead

effects.log: You lie down outside a house in the dark, though they have barred the door, and eat the bad dream of a child inside. It tastes, very faintly, of rice. (Rice +3)

events.text: The last grains in your tail are going. You can feel them going, one by one, turning to iron. Nothing in you remembers a pair of hands, except one grain, very faintly, which you could still save, if you gave back enough, if you ate something that was not iron.

choices.text: Give back everything you took this century

effects.log: You give back everything you took this century, at every door, in one long night of walking. In the morning the last grain is still rice, and so is the one beside it. (Rice +6)

choices.text: Go and find the river towns, and eat their bad dreams

effects.log: You go back down the river, house by house, as you did once, and eat the bad dreams, and the tail warms, a grain at a time. (Rice +5)

choices.text: Let the last grain go

effects.log: You let it go. The last grain turns to iron, and nothing in you remembers a pair of hands. You eat until there is no iron in the land, and then lie down in a field of rust under a red sky, and the old proverb is about you, for ever: Songdo's last-days beast, that would not stop.

events.text: Fire is food to you now, and the court has forgotten that it ever was not. But somebody at court has read the old books, the ones that say the beast no blade can kill can be killed by fire, and has noticed one line: at the tail. Torches are being bought in the capital by the cartload.

choices.text: Go and eat the torches before they are lit

effects.log: You go into the capital at night and eat the torch-stores, and the oil jars, and the trench-diggers' spades. The court finds out what you think of its plan. It is very afraid, and more determined. (Fear +3)

choices.text: Let them come

effects.log: Let them come. You have eaten a palace fire. You lie on your hill and wait, and keep your tail curled under you.

events.text: They come at night: a ring of soldiers with torches, a trench dug round your hill and filled with oil, and archers with fire-arrows who know where to aim. The trench goes up all at once. Through the smoke you see the arrows turning, all of them, toward your tail.

choices.text: Eat the fire, all of it

ok.log: You eat it: the trench, the arrows, the torches out of their hands. It goes into you like a river into the sea. The soldiers stand in the dark holding sticks. Your tail is not even warm. (Heat +20)

fail.log: You eat most of it. One fire-arrow finds the tail, and the rice there scorches black at the tip before you can put it out. It hurts in a way nothing has hurt for four hundred years. (Rice -6)

choices.text: Walk through the ring and away

effects.log: You walk through the ring of soldiers and away, slowly, with your tail curled up under you, and nobody can reach it. They follow you for a month and give up. (Rice -1)

events.text: They come again, years later, more of them, and this time they have dug the trench in the night while you slept in the old mine, and the fire is already in the tail before you are awake. The rice is burning. It is not like being given back. It is like being taken.

choices.text: Plunge the tail into the river

effects.log: You go down the hillside into the river in three strides and sit in it, steaming, until the fire is out. The rice is black at the tip. It will grow back, slowly, if you are good to it. (Rice -5)

choices.text: Eat the fire out of your own tail

effects.log: You curl round and draw the fire out of your own tail through your trunk, which nothing has ever done. It goes down bitter. The rice is scorched, but it is there. The soldiers drop their torches and run. (Rice -3)

choices.text: Do not turn in time

effects.log: You do not turn in time. Perhaps you are too old; perhaps you are tired. The fire takes the rice, against your will, and the iron pours out of you onto an empty field: needles, ploughs, bells, swords, all of it, with nobody there to carry any of it home.

events.text: Nine swords given. You wake one morning on the valley floor below the sect mountains, and something has changed, and it takes you all day to understand what. Nobody has drawn a blade at you for a year. Not one.

choices.text: Lie still and listen to the valley

effects.log: You listen: hammers in the smithies, making ploughs. Wooden swords clacking in the sect courtyards. Children. Somebody singing. No steel drawn anywhere you can hear. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Walk through the nearest sect gate, to see

effects.log: You walk in through the nearest sect gate. The disciples look up from their wooden swords, and wave, and go on practising. The master on the steps nods to you as to a neighbour. (Rice +2)

events.text: The sects of the valley practise with wooden swords now. Not because they have none: the forges still make steel, for knives and kitchens. They practise with wood because there is nothing left in the world that anyone wants to use steel on.

choices.text: Watch a class of beginners

effects.log: You watch a class of beginners all morning. They are terrible. They are terrible in exactly the way beginners were terrible once, when the swords were real, and it is a joy to watch.

choices.text: Offer the masters their old blades back to teach with

effects.log: You offer the masters the blades back, to teach with. The masters talk about it for a season and say no, thank you, the wood is enough. One of them asks instead if you would lie still while the beginners practise climbing. (Rice +2)

events.text: The children of the valley have found out that if you climb all the way up your back, past the hilts, past the needles, to the top of your head, you can see the sea. They come up in groups on clear days, in a long line, holding on to the hilts like the rungs of a ladder.

choices.text: Hold very still for them

effects.log: You hold very still, every clear day, for generations of children. You never shift. Not once does one of them fall. In the valley, a child who has seen the sea from your head is counted grown. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Lift them the last part with your trunk

effects.log: You lift the small ones the last part with your trunk, very gently, and set them on your head. They scream with joy. The sea is very far, very bright. (Rice +2)

events.text: A great master comes from far away, very young, very good, with a sword. Not to take anything back. To find out, the master says, whether the beast no blade can kill can still be fought. The valley stops to watch, uneasy.

choices.text: Fight, once, for the joy of it

ok.log: You fight, for an afternoon, and it is the best fight in five hundred years, and nobody is hurt, and at the end you eat the sword very politely and give it back. The young master laughs until sitting down is necessary. (Rice +1)

fail.log: The young master is better than you thought, and lands a cut that you feel, a long shallow one, on the shoulder. You laugh, which shakes the valley. The master bows. Nobody has done that to you in ages. (-6 health)

choices.text: Lie still and let the blade find nothing to cut

effects.log: You lie still. The young master cuts, and cuts, and every cut goes into you like a spoon into rice, and comes out clean, and you do not even look up. After an hour the master sheathes the sword, and sits down beside the children, and stays in the valley. (Rice +2)

events.text: You could live like this a thousand years more, and you might. The sects keep wooden swords. The smiths make ploughs. There is no blade anywhere in the land that anyone would raise against you, because there is nothing left that anyone wants to raise one for. You are what the old name always meant, after all.

choices.text: Wander the land a while longer

effects.log: You get up, and the children slide down, and you go for a walk across the land, a century or two. Everywhere you go, nobody draws. You will come back to the valley. You always do.

choices.text: Go and eat a few bad dreams in the river towns

effects.log: You go down the river and eat bad dreams, as you did when you were young, house by house. Some things you never stop doing because you stopped needing to. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Lie down in the valley, and be the Unkillable

effects.log: You lie down in the sunlit valley among the sect halls, with a hundred hilts on your back and the children climbing you to see the sea, and you are the Unkillable: not the beast no blade can kill, but the beast no blade is raised against. You sleep. You are not asleep. You are exactly where you are.

events.text: You dream, one night, of the room where you were made: the boards, the lamp, the smell of old rice and a tired person's breath. In the dream you are a few grains on the floor, and nothing has happened yet, and a pair of hands is about to reach down. You wake with the taste of rice in your trunk, and an ache like homesickness.

choices.text: Try to dream it again

effects.log: You try. For a year you sleep only to dream it, and sometimes you do. The hands are always about to reach down. They never quite do. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Go and find a room like it in a village, and look

effects.log: You find a farmhouse with a loft and put one eye to the gap in the thatch. Boards, a lamp, nothing. A family's old chests. You look a long time. (Rice +1)

events.text: A wind comes down out of heaven, not a storm, a broom: the kind of wind that sweeps a floor clean. It is sweeping toward you across the valley. You can feel, without knowing how, that if you let it, it will sweep you up and set you down a few grains on a floor in lamplight, remembering everything, at the very beginning.

choices.text: Hold your ground

effects.log: You hold your ground, a mountain against a broom. The wind goes round you, and on, and away. You stay what you are, with everything you have done in you. (Rice +1)

choices.text: Ask the wind to come back another century

effects.log: You ask it, and it seems to listen; at least it goes. You do not know if it will come back. You think it might, if you ask.

choices.text: Let it sweep you up

effects.log: You let it. It sweeps you up, all the iron, all the swords, all the centuries, and somewhere in the sweeping they fall away, and you are a few grains of cooked rice on a dusty floor in lamplight, remembering everything. Above you, very far up, a pair of hands is about to reach down.

events.text: {npc} is a ferryman on the great river who has ferried you across, or tried to, every spring for thirty years: you wade, and {npc} rows beside you and talks. Today {npc} rows you to a place under the cliffs where the water is black and very still. "The deepest pool on the river," {npc} says. "Nobody knows the bottom. I come here to think."

choices.text: Stand there a while with {him}

effects.log: You stand in the black water beside the boat, the whole mountain of you, with only your trunk and eyes above it, and {npc} rows in slow circles and says nothing. It is the quietest afternoon of your life. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Dive, to see the bottom

effects.log: You dive. The bottom is a very long way down, and dark, and cold, and full of anchors, which you eat. When you come up {npc} is laughing so hard the boat is rocking.

events.text: {npc} is old now, and has asked to be rowed to the deep pool one last time, by you this time, pushing the boat with your trunk. When you get there {npc} looks down into the black water for a long time. "I always thought," {npc} says, "that something as big as you could rest down there. Nobody would find you. You could just listen."

choices.text: Push the boat home

effects.log: You push the boat home, slowly, so {npc} can watch the cliffs go by. That evening {npc} gives you the old oar, for luck. You eat it, eventually, many years later, when you miss {him} most.

choices.text: Listen to the pool a while with {him}, and go

effects.log: You stay a while, listening to the pool, both of you. It is very quiet down there; you can feel it. Then you take {npc} home. You will come back. (Rice +1)

choices.text: Follow {him} into the pool, and sink

effects.log: {npc} steps out of the boat into the black water, and you follow, and you sink together, slowly, into the deepest pool on the river. The ferry drifts home on its own. On quiet nights, ever after, the ferrymen hear something chewing an anchor down in the dark, very contentedly, and two voices, talking.

events.text: Something falls out of the sky over the eastern ridge, very fast, trailing light: a flying sword, an immortal's, dropped or lost or thrown in a quarrel among the clouds. It is coming down straight at you. It smells of iron and of something better than iron.

choices.text: Open your jaws

effects.log: You open your jaws, and it goes in, and it is the best thing you have ever eaten: iron from a forge in the clouds, light and cold and full of qi. You glow for a month. (+qi)

choices.text: Catch it in your trunk and hold it up for its owner

effects.log: You catch it in your trunk and hold it up to the sky. A long while later an immortal comes down, very embarrassed, and takes it back, and thanks you, and asks your name. (Rice +2)

events.text: An immortal envoy comes down on a cloud with a scroll, and reads it out from a safe height: heaven's armoury has noticed you. Heaven would like to know what you intend to eat next. Heaven would like it in writing.

choices.text: Say: only what is given

effects.log: "Only what is given," you say. The envoy writes it down, looks at it, and asks if heaven may give you something. You say heaven may try. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Say: bad dreams, mostly

effects.log: "Bad dreams, mostly," you say. The envoy writes it down, frowns, and asks, in a much smaller voice, whether you would come up one night: heaven has some. (Rice +1)

choices.text: Eat the envoy's cloud-chariot's fittings

effects.log: You eat the bronze fittings off the envoy's cloud-chariot. The envoy goes back up holding the cloud together by hand. Heaven does not ask again for a century. (Rice -1)

events.text: Heaven sends a gift: one sword from the armoury in the clouds, carried down by three immortals in a procession, held out to you hilt-first over the valley. It is the first gift heaven has ever sent to anything that was not a god.

choices.text: Take it, as given

effects.log: You take it. It counts. It goes into you like starlight into a well. The three immortals bow, unsure of the etiquette, and go back up. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Send it back to heaven with thanks

effects.log: You send it back with thanks: heaven needs its swords more than you do, you say, which heaven finds so astonishing that the story is told in the courts above for a thousand years.

events.text: There are so many voices in you now: every sword's old owner, every general, every master, every soldier whose spear you ate. At night they talk among themselves, and argue, and sometimes sing. Tonight they are arguing about you.

choices.text: Listen to the argument

effects.log: You listen. Half of them think you should stop. Half think you should never stop. One old general thinks you should invade the north. A cook whose cleaver you ate thinks you should eat less. You agree with the cook.

choices.text: Tell them all to be quiet

effects.log: You tell them to be quiet, in your own voice, the one that is a scrap of rice. They are quiet. It is the first silence inside you in two hundred years, and you sleep a whole week in it.

events.text: One of the voices in you is very old and very quiet and belongs to nobody you ate: it was there before the first needle. It does not argue with the others. It only says, now and then, when they have finished: enough.

choices.text: Ask it what is enough

effects.log: You ask. It does not answer. It only says, again, very gently: enough. You think about that for a long time, and you think it means you will know.

choices.text: Answer it: not yet

effects.log: Not yet, you tell it. It does not argue. It never does. It only waits, which is worse.

events.text: A swordsman's voice in you, one of the oldest, asks you one night to go back to a grave and give the sword back. It is the first time any of them has asked for anything.

choices.text: Go and give it back

effects.log: You go to a grave in the south, under a pine, and open your jaws, and lay the sword on the mound. The voice in you sighs, and goes quiet, and does not speak again. You miss it a little. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Keep it: you need its art

effects.log: You keep it. You need its art. The voice does not ask again, but you can feel it there, disappointed, like a stone in a shoe. (Rice -1)

events.text: The Demonic Cult has heard that the murim is giving you its swords, and sends its own, unasked: the Blood Blade, red and humming, laid on a black cloth on a rock in front of you by an envoy who does not stay. It is given. Whether it is a gift is another matter.

choices.text: Eat it

effects.log: You eat it. It goes down hot and humming and red, and something in your tail shrinks from it, the way a hand shrinks from a stove. It does not count as given. Nothing the Cult gives freely is free. (Rice -3)

choices.text: Leave it on the rock

effects.log: You leave it on the rock. In the morning it is gone; the Cult has taken it back, or someone else has. You feel lighter for not knowing. (Rice +1)

choices.text: Push it into the deep river

effects.log: You push it into the deepest part of the river with your trunk. The water steams for a week. Fishermen downstream catch red fish for a year, and throw them back. (Rice +2)

events.text: The Blood Blade is in you, and you can feel it, at night, talking to the other swords in a voice like a coal. It tells them they could take everything. Some of them are listening.

choices.text: Spit it out on the Cult's doorstep

effects.log: You walk to the Cult's mountain and spit it out on the steps of their hall at noon. They do not come out. It lies there, red, until someone dares to pick it up. Your tail warms by evening. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Keep it, and keep it quiet

effects.log: You keep it, and every night you tell it to be quiet, and every night it is a little less quiet. It is a strong blade. It is a strong blade. (Rice -1)

events.text: The general's sword is in you, the one who looked on gold as stone, who died when the old kingdom fell. People say no grass ever grew on his grave, for the wrong done to him. You have not been to see it in a very long time.

choices.text: Go and see it

effects.log: You go. The grave is red earth, bare, on a hillside where everything else is green. You lie beside it a night. In the morning there is one blade of grass on it, very small. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Not yet

effects.log: Not yet. The general's sword stirs in you, once, and is still. It has waited centuries; it can wait.

events.text: At the red grave again. The general's sword has been quiet in you a long time, but here it stirs.

choices.text: Lay the sword on the grave and leave it

effects.log: You lay it on the grave. It is the general's; it should be with him. Grass grows on the grave that spring, all at once, green to the edges. You have one relic fewer, and you do not feel smaller. (Rice +4)

choices.text: Keep it, and promise the general a better use

effects.log: You keep it, and promise the general, out loud, at the graveside, to use his sword only as he would have: looking on gold as stone. The red earth says nothing. (Rice +1)

events.text: A sect leader has come to you alone with a sword: {npc}, whose sect has been at war with its neighbour for twenty years. "Take it," {npc} says. "If it is in you, I cannot use it, and the war is over. I cannot stop myself any other way."

choices.text: Take it, as given

effects.log: You take it. {npc} stands on the path with empty hands and weeps with relief, and goes home, and makes peace that winter. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Ask {him} to stop without you

effects.log: You ask {npc} to try to stop without you first. {npc} goes home and tries, and fails, and comes back the next year, and you take it then. It counts more, somehow. (Rice +3)

events.text: A grandmaster at the very top of the world below has come to stand in front of you: {npc}, who wants to be the one blade you cannot eat. "Try," says {npc}, and draws.

choices.text: Try

ok.log: You try, and after a long hard morning you have the sword, very gently, out of {npc}'s hand. {npc} looks at the empty hand and laughs. You give it back. It was never the blade that could not be eaten; it was the hand. (Rice +1)

fail.log: You try, all morning, and you cannot: the blade moves faster than your jaws, every time. {npc} sheathes it at noon, and bows, and goes. You will remember that blade. (-5 health)

choices.text: Decline: some blades should stay uneaten

effects.log: You decline. "Some blades," you say, in the voice of an old master, "should stay where they are." {npc} lowers the sword, offended and then, slowly, pleased.

events.text: A disciple has come up the hill because people say a dead master's voice comes out of you: {npc}, who buried that master forty years ago and never said goodbye.

choices.text: Speak in the master's voice

effects.log: You find the voice among the others, and speak in it. {npc} sits down in the grass and listens, and answers, and says goodbye. It takes until dark. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Say gently that it is only an echo

effects.log: You tell {npc} the truth: it is only an echo, the shape a voice leaves in a sword. {npc} nods, and asks to hear the echo anyway. You let {him}. (Rice +1)

events.text: {npc}, a human at the height of the world, has come to sit with you, not to fight or to give. "I am as far as a human goes," says {npc}. "So are you, nearly, as far as whatever you are goes. I thought I might stop. I thought you might know how."

choices.text: Say: I am learning, too

effects.log: "I am learning too," you say. You sit together on the hill for a year, two creatures at the top of everything, practising stopping. Neither of you is good at it. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Show {him} a bowl of rice, and eat it slowly

effects.log: You do not answer. You eat a bowl of rice someone left you, grain by grain, very slowly, for an hour. {npc} watches the whole time, and at the end says, "Oh." (Rice +2)

events.text: An immortal envoy has come down on a cloud to ask, very formally, what you will eat next: {npc}, with a scroll and a brush and a cloud-chariot with no metal in it at all, on purpose.

choices.text: Say: nothing that is not given

effects.log: "Nothing that is not given," you say. {npc} writes it down, and looks at the cloud-chariot, and looks a little disappointed that the precaution was unneeded.

choices.text: Say: whatever heaven is afraid of

effects.log: "Whatever heaven is afraid of," you say. {npc} drops the brush. You give it back. You are, you discover, enjoying yourself.

events.text: A heavenly immortal stands before you with a handful of rusty nails held out: {npc}, who was once, many lives and a heaven ago, a child in a village who fed you nails from a flat palm.

choices.text: Eat the nails from {his} hand

effects.log: You eat the nails from {npc}'s palm, one by one, the way you did when you were small. {npc} laughs like a child. Heaven is very far away for an afternoon. (Rice +3)

choices.text: Ask what heaven is like

effects.log: You ask. {npc} thinks, and says it is like the village, but nobody feeds anything nails. You both think that is a pity.

events.text: A sovereign of a high heaven has come down in state: {npc}, who has a rival heaven with a famous armoury, and would like you to go and eat it. "Name your price," says {npc}.

choices.text: Refuse: you eat only what is given

effects.log: You refuse. {npc} offers more. You refuse more. In the end {npc} goes back up, furious, and the rival heaven never knows how close it came.

choices.text: Ask the rival heaven first if it would give

effects.log: You go up and ask the rival heaven, politely, if it would give you its armoury. It says no. You tell {npc} that you asked, and it said no, and that is the end of it. {npc} has never heard of anything so absurd. (Rice +2)

events.text: A child has walked up the hill alone with a bad dream and asks you to eat it: {npc}, nine years old, who has heard you do that. The dream is of a dog that bit {him} last summer. It is quite a small dream.

choices.text: Eat it, there and then

effects.log: You put your trunk very gently to {npc}'s forehead and draw it out: a small dream, a dog, a summer. It tastes of nothing and then of a child who is not afraid of dogs any more. {npc} walks home without looking back. (Rice +2)

choices.text: Leave half, so {he} remembers to be careful of dogs
